The DOORS are attested reading-traditions surfaced from the retrieved reception store (~/reception-corpus), NOT authored from recall; every witness `reading` is the source's own words, lightly trimmed (Glossa editorial source-markers like ((BEDA.)) dropped; the Migne recension's own 'etc., as far as' abridgements are marked with '...'). The editorial framing (trap/hinge/gravity/synthesis/claim/say/do/subtract) is AI-drafted and pending Wilson's curation. [Authored 2026-10-06, Opus, Phase 4b brief, born v2: the build carries one track ('single'), first reading 2 Samuel 7:1-11, 16 with the Magnificat (Luke 1:46b-55) in the psalm slot. The Gospel, Luke 1:26-38, is a single span, so only `refKey` is set. The store has NO Catena Aurea Fathers on Luke 1:26-38 (Barnes, Calvin, JFB and Matthew Henry are index-only rows with no text; Barth CD rows not used), so the Gospel doors rest on the Glossa ordinaria (Migne) 1:27, 1:29, 1:30, 1:35, 1:36, 1:38, Wesley's Notes 1:28, 1:35, 1:38, and Catena intertext notes on 1:26-33 (Judges 6:12, Zephaniah 3:14-17) and 1:34-38 (Exodus 40:35, Genesis 18:14, 1 Samuel 1:11). 2 Samuel 7 is split (1-11, 16); `firstReading.refKeys` carries both spans, and the turn_pull dump covered both. Its doors draw on Glossa 7:3, 7:16, Wesley 7:3, 7:4, 7:8, 7:11, 7:16, and Catena intertext notes (taken up at Acts 7:44-50, Luke 1:26-33). Of the Glossa 7:16 row only the first gloss is used; its two further lemmas ('And he sat before', 'The law of Adam') belong to 7:18-19, outside the lection. Glossa 7:10 (Solomon's peace) and the many 'Son of David' intertext notes on 7:12-16 were left aside. Magnificat rows (Glossa 1:47, 1:48, 1:53; Wesley 1:47, 1:51-52) inform gravity/synthesis only.]
trap: Mary becomes a model of the right attitude: be open, be willing, say yes to God, and the sermon turns her consent into a technique for receiving blessings. Or the Annunciation becomes a pageant tableau, lit and costumed and four days before Christmas, so lovely that nobody notices a girl from a nowhere town being told something that cannot happen.
hinge: Everything in the story is God's initiative: the angel sent, the favour given, the Spirit coming, the power overshadowing, the child named before he is conceived. And still the story waits on one sentence from a troubled young woman. The preacher has to hold both: grace that needs no help, and a yes that is really asked for.

doors.claim: Mary's answer is not a claim to greatness but a confession of who she is before God: his servant. Her yes is humble faith that wants God's promise done, and the same posture Hannah took when she prayed for a son.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Behold the handmaid of the Lord. She does not exalt herself for the singularity of her merit, but, mindful in all things of her own condition and of the divine kinship, she confesses herself to be the handmaid of him whose mother she is chosen to be, and with great devotion desires the angel's promise to be fulfilled.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord — It is not improbable, that this time of the virgin's humble faith, consent, and expectation, might be the very time of her conceiving.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: To a virgin. A woman seduced by the devil brought in death: on the contrary, a woman taught by an angel brought forth salvation.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Behold, the handmaid (doule) of the Lord' takes up Hannah's self-designation as 'your handmaid' before the Lord (1 Samuel 1:11). The humble servant-woman posture coheres with the Hannah/Magnificat substratum that crystallizes a few verses later. (Allusion of 1 Samuel 1:11)

doors.say: Mary does not say 'I am ready' or 'I am worthy.' She says whose she is. Faith begins there, not with how much you can handle but with whom you belong to.
doors.do: Ask them to pray Mary's sentence, 'Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word,' each morning this week, and to notice where in the day it is hardest to mean.

doors.landing: The power of the Most High will overshadow you
doors.claim: The child is not Mary's achievement. The Spirit comes upon her and the power of God overshadows her as the glory-cloud covered the tabernacle. What God promised to the barren Sarah and the old Elizabeth he does again: nothing he speaks is impossible.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee — The power of God was put forth by the Holy Ghost, as the immediate Divine agent in this work: and so he exerted the power of the Highest as his own power, who together with the Father and the Son is the most high God.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: The Holy One shall be called the Son of God. Jesus is born holy, who was to overcome the condition of corruptible nature, and he was not conceived by the mingling of carnal union. We, bound fast by the condition of corruptible nature, can be sanctified through grace.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'The power of the Most High will overshadow (episkiasei) you' uses the verb for the glory-cloud that 'overshadowed' the tent of meeting when the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35 LXX). The distinctive Shekinah-overshadowing diction frames Mary as the dwelling place of God's presence. (Allusion of Exodus 40:35)

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And behold. Lest the virgin should despair of the childbearing ... she might know that the forerunner too was to be born of a barren old woman.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'For everything spoken by God is possible' answers the rhetorical question to Abraham and Sarah, 'Is anything too hard (impossible, LXX) for the Lord?' (Genesis 18:14), in the very context of a miraculous conception by an old, barren woman. (Allusion of Genesis 18:14)

doors.say: Mary asks how this can be, and the answer is not a method but a presence: the same glory that filled the tent will fill her. What God has said, God can do, in a barren woman, in a virgin, in you.
doors.do: Invite them to name one thing in their life they have filed under 'impossible' and to bring it to God in prayer this week with Gabriel's sentence: nothing will be impossible with God.

doors.landing: Fear not: the Lord is with thee
doors.claim: Mary is troubled, and the angel calls her by name and tells her not to be afraid. 'The Lord is with you' is what God said to Gideon hiding in a winepress and to daughter Zion in her fear. Favour here is not a halo but a calling given to someone shaken.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: She was troubled. Because she did not know whether what the angel said was past or to come. ... Fear not, Mary. Her, troubled by the unwonted salutation, he calls by name as one more familiarly known. He bids her not to fear, and more fully explains why he had called her full of grace.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Thou art highly favoured, or hast found favour with God, ver. 30, is no more than was said of Noah, Moses, and David. The Lord is with thee, was said to Gideon, Judg. vi, 12; and blessed shall she be above women, of Jael, Judg. v, 24.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'The Lord is with you' reproduces the angel's salutation to Gideon, 'The Lord is with you, mighty man of valor' (Judges 6:12), within a near-identical commissioning-of-a-deliverer scene including a 'how can this be' objection. (Allusion of Judges 6:12)

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'Rejoice (chaire)... the Lord is with you' echoes the address to Daughter Zion: 'Rejoice, O Daughter of Zion... the Lord your God is in your midst' (Zephaniah 3:14-17 LXX). The greeting-rejoice + indwelling-Lord pairing casts Mary figurally as Zion. (Allusion of Zephaniah 3:14-17)

doors.say: The first thing heaven says to Mary after hello is 'Do not be afraid.' God's favour does not find people calm and ready. It finds them troubled, calls them by name, and says, I am with you.
doors.do: Have them name the fear they are carrying into Christmas, write 'The Lord is with you' beside it, and keep the note where they will see it every day until the 25th.

doors.landing: Go, do all that is in your heart
doors.claim: David's plan is pious and Nathan blesses it on the spot, and both are wrong. The prophet spoke from his own spirit before he had asked God. God corrects a good intention gently, but he does correct it.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Nathan said — Pursue thy intentions, and build an house for the ark. The design being pious and the thing not forbidden by God, Nathan hastily approves it, before he had consulted God about it, as both he and David ought to have done in a matter of so great moment. ... For the holy prophets did not speak all things by prophetic inspiration, but some things by an human spirit.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: All that is in thy heart, go and do. It is plain that the spirit of prophecy does not always irradiate the minds of the prophets. ... while he gives and withdraws the spirit of prophecy, he lifts up the minds of those who prophesy on high, and keeps them in humility, so that, receiving the spirit, they may find what they are of God, and again, not having the spirit of prophecy, they may know what they are of themselves.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The word of the Lord came — Because David's mistake was pious, and from an honest mind, God would not suffer him to lie long in it.

doors.say: Not every good idea is God's idea, even when the pastor says yes. God loves David enough to stop him, and he does it the same night.
doors.do: Ask them to take one good plan they are carrying into the new year and, before they start it, to pray over it and ask God plainly whether it is theirs to build.

doors.landing: The Lord will make you a house
doors.claim: David wants to build God a house, and God turns the offer around: you will not build me a house; I will build you one. God has never asked for a cedar dwelling; he gives his servant rest, a people, and a dynasty.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He will, &c. - For thy good intentions to make him an house, he will make thee an house, a sure house, that is, he will increase and uphold thy posterity, and continue thy kingdom in thy family.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: My servant — Lest David should be too much discouraged, or judge himself neglected of God, as one thought unworthy of so great an honour, God here gives him the honourable title of his servant, thereby signifying that he accepted of his service, and good intentions.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: David 'asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob' alludes to David's wish to build a house for the ark, the occasion of Nathan's oracle. (taken up at Acts 7:44-50)

doors.say: David offered God a house and God said no, and then said something better: I will build you one. The gospel always runs that direction, from God to us.
doors.do: Invite them to list what they are trying to build for God this season and then, beside it, what God has already built for them, and to give thanks for the second list first.

doors.landing: Your throne shall be established for ever
doors.claim: The promise of an everlasting house and throne outruns Solomon and every son of David after him. The church hears it truly said of Christ, and Gabriel quotes it to Mary: of his kingdom there will be no end.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: And faithful. This is truly said of Christ ... the place therefore of so peaceful and secure a dwelling is eternal, where the true Israel shall be, that is, he that seeth God.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Before thee — Thine eyes in some sort beholding it ... especially considering that he had his eyes and thoughts upon the Messiah, Psalm cx, 1, &c. whose day he saw by faith, as Abraham did, John viii, 56, and whom he knew that God would raise out of the fruit of his loins to sit on his throne, and that forever: and so the eternity of his kingdom is rightly said to be before him.

witnesses.author: Catena — intertextual
witnesses.reading: 'The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign... forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom' is built on the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7:12-16, where God establishes David's offspring and 'his throne forever.' (taken up at Luke 1:26-33)

doors.say: God promised David a king who would never be replaced. Every king of Judah fell short of it, and then an angel walked into Nazareth and said: this is the one.
doors.do: Have them read 2 Samuel 7:16 and Luke 1:32-33 side by side this week and name one place in their life where they need to hear that his kingdom, not theirs and not any other, has no end.

single.gravity: Advent's last Sunday stands at the door. David, settled in his cedar house, wants to build God one, and God answers through Nathan: you will not build me a house; I will build you a house, and your throne shall stand for ever (2 Samuel 7). Mary sings that the Mighty One has looked on the lowliness of his servant, scattered the proud, filled the hungry, and remembered his promise to Abraham (Luke 1:46b-55). Paul gives glory to God for the mystery kept secret for long ages and now disclosed (Romans 16). And Gabriel tells a girl in Nazareth that her son will sit on David's throne. The nerve: the house God promised David is built not by a king's ambition but in a servant's body, and the dwelling God would not let David build he builds himself.

synthesis.convergence: David offers God a house and is told God will build him one, a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7). Mary praises the God who lifts the lowly and keeps his promise to the fathers (Luke 1:46b-55). Paul names a mystery hidden for ages and now revealed (Romans 16). Gabriel announces that the Spirit will overshadow Mary and her son will take David's throne (Luke 1). Every reading has God doing the building: the promise to David, kept in the handmaid.
synthesis.claim: God does not wait for us to build him a house; he makes his dwelling among us by his own power, and he chooses the lowly to carry it.
synthesis.here: For a congregation four days from Christmas, likely tired from building the perfect holiday, the move is from David's cedar-house project to Mary's sentence. The work that matters this week is not what we make for God but what we let him do in us: Here am I; let it be with me.

subtract: These three are doors, not points. Each is a different landing: Mary's humble yes as the servant of the Lord, the Spirit's overshadowing power for which nothing is impossible, and God's 'do not be afraid' to someone troubled. Walk through one and let the other two go; the choosing is the sermon's focus.
source: Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and Catena intertextual notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus. Attested, not authored. (No Catena Aurea Fathers are on file for Luke 1:26-38.)
